337.title: Not good to be alone (Genesis 2:18–25)
337.hook: the only thing in creation God calls not good is loneliness
337.carry: bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh
337.howItsDone: Genesis 2:18–24 is one of the Old Testament readings Catholic couples can choose for their wedding Mass, and the Church reads it as the beginning of marriage and of all human community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adamah: clay on a workbench, and God's breath, face to face. Your line was dust that breathes. A new week starts.

Count the verdicts so far. Light: good. Dry land and sea: good. Plants: good. Sun, moon and stars: good. Fish and birds, cattle and creeping things: good. Everything together: very good. Genesis keeps saying it like a bell. Then, in the garden, with the first human freshly made and a whole world to tend, the bell rings wrong. God looks at the man and says something is not good. Not sin. No serpent, no fruit, nothing has gone wrong yet. Just one person, by himself, in paradise.
screen: `GOOD, GOOD, GOOD, VERY GOOD.` → `THE BELL RINGS WRONG.` → `ONE PERSON, BY HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "It is not good for man to be alone: let us make him a help like unto himself." The first thing in the Bible called not good isn't evil. It's being alone. The man has God, a garden and work, and still something is missing. Then the word help. In Hebrew it's ezer kenegdo, a helper corresponding to him, one who stands facing him. Ezer is not a servant's word: the Hebrew Bible uses it most often for God, who is Israel's help. So the help God promises isn't an assistant. It's a partner, an equal, someone who can look back. Next, the search. God brings the animals to the man, and he names every one, cattle, birds, beasts of the field, but none of them is the help like himself. So God casts the man into a deep sleep, takes one of his ribs, closes up the flesh, and builds a woman. When he wakes and sees her, the first human words in the Bible spill out, close to a song: this now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. The Catechism says man and woman are made for each other, a communion of persons, and that this is where marriage begins. But the Church also reads the line more widely: no human being is made to be alone. Friendship, family, parish, neighbors: all of them answer the same not good. And the scene ends quietly. They were both naked, and were not ashamed.

338.title: The serpent (Genesis 3:1–7)
338.hook: did God really say, and the fruit that looked good
338.howItsDone: Catholics pray "lead us not into temptation" in every Our Father, and the Church reads Genesis 3 on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, as Lent begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ezer kenegdo: the first not good, and an equal who stands facing him. Your line was bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh.

segments.voice: Plenty of paintings of this scene share the same props: a tree, a woman reaching up, a shiny red apple, maybe a snake curled around a branch, with a face. Open Genesis and look for the apple. It isn't there. The text just says fruit. Some readers think the apple grew later, in art, perhaps helped along by a Latin pun: malum means evil, and malum also means apple. The real story is quieter and stranger. It doesn't start with a bite. It starts with a question.
screen: `A TREE, A WOMAN, A RED APPLE.` → `THE TEXT SAYS ONLY FRUIT.` → `IT STARTS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The serpent, Genesis says, was more subtle than any of the beasts, and its first words are a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?" Other translations put it more sharply: did God really say? God had said they could eat of every tree but one. The serpent turns the one limit into the whole story. The woman corrects it, but now the doubt is in the air. Then the serpent goes further: you won't die; God knows that you'll be like gods. That's the shape of temptation the Church sees here. First, a question that shrinks the gift and enlarges the rule. Then the suspicion: maybe God is holding out on you. Then the look. The tree is good to eat, fair to the eyes, desirable for wisdom. In the story, the wrong choice shows up looking good. She eats, gives some to her husband, who is with her, and he eats. Their eyes are opened, but all they see is that they're naked. They sew fig leaves. The Catechism reads this as the first sin: letting trust in God die in the heart, and wanting to be like God without God. It uses figurative language, the Catechism says, but it tells of a real event at the start of human history. Genesis never names the serpent. Later scripture fills that in: the Book of Wisdom says death came into the world by the envy of the devil, and Revelation calls the devil that old serpent.

339.title: Where art thou (Genesis 3:8–13)
339.hook: God walks in the garden in the cool of the day and calls for the hiding couple
339.howItsDone: In the sacrament of reconciliation, Catholics name their own sins aloud to a priest, rather than explaining others' faults, and receive absolution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, temptation: a question that makes the gift look small. Your line was did god really say. Today, what happens right after the bite.

A kid breaks a vase. The parent hears the crash from the kitchen, walks into the living room, and the room is empty. Except for two small feet sticking out from behind the curtain. Everyone knows exactly where the child is. And still the parent says, out loud, gently or not: where are you? That's Genesis today. The fruit is eaten, the fig leaves are sewn, and the evening breeze comes through the garden, and with it, the sound of someone walking.
screen: `A CRASH, AN EMPTY ROOM.` → `TWO FEET BEHIND THE CURTAIN.` → `SOMEONE WALKING IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: First, the walk. Genesis says the man and the woman heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden, in the afternoon air, the cool of the day. It's an astonishingly close picture of God: not thunder, but footsteps at evening, as if this were a habit. And they hide among the trees. Then the question. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God called Adam, and said to him: Where art thou?" In Hebrew it's one word, ayekkah. God made the man from dust; God isn't asking for directions. Teachers in both Jewish and Christian tradition have read it this way: the question is for Adam, a chance to come out on his own. His answer is painfully honest: "I heard thy voice in paradise; and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." Afraid, naked, hid. No excuses yet. Then the blame. God asks who told him he was naked, and whether he ate. The man points: the woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit. He blames her and, quietly, God too. The woman points at the serpent. Nobody says I did it. The Catechism says the harmony of the garden is broken here: between the man and woman, with creation, and with God. And yet God's first word to the man who has hidden is not a sentence. It's a question that goes looking for him. Catholics hear the same call in confession: come out from behind the trees and say it.

340.title: The first good news (Genesis 3:15)
340.hook: even in the curse, a promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent; Catholics see Christ and Mary here
340.howItsDone: Genesis 3:9–15, 20 is read at Mass on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, December 8, and some Catholic images of Mary show the serpent under her feet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayekkah: footsteps in the evening, and a question that went looking for someone hiding. Your line was afraid, naked, hid.

A statue of Mary stands in a side chapel. She's on a globe, hands open or folded, and under her bare feet, crushed flat, there's a snake, sometimes with an apple in its mouth. Statues like this turn up in Catholic churches and on holy cards, easy to pass without a second look. But that snake under her heel is a Bible verse turned into stone. It comes from a dark moment in Genesis: the fruit eaten, the blame passed around, God about to speak the consequences. And tucked into the sentence on the serpent comes a promise.
screen: `MARY ON A GLOBE.` → `A SNAKE UNDER HER HEEL.` → `A VERSE TURNED INTO STONE.`

segments.voice: God turns first to the serpent, curses it to crawl on its belly, and then says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel." First, the order. Before God says a word to the man or the woman about pain and sweat and dust, God promises that evil won't win. The promise comes before their sentences. Second, the name. Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus read this verse as pointing to Christ, and the Catechism calls it the protoevangelium, the first announcement of the good news. The woman's seed will crush the serpent's head, while the serpent only strikes the heel: a wound, but not a fatal one. Third, the word she. The Hebrew says he, or it, the offspring. The Greek Old Testament says he. Saint Jerome's Latin Vulgate has ipsa, she, and the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, follows it. Modern Catholic translations such as the New American Bible follow the Hebrew. Fourth, how the Church holds both. The Catechism reads the verse as pointing to Christ, the new Adam, and to Mary, the new Eve, who shares in his victory. So the Church doesn't need to choose between he and she: the Son crushes the serpent, and his mother stands with him. That's the statue: the promise of Genesis three, carved in stone where you'd pass it.

341.title: Am I my brother's keeper (Genesis 4:1–16)
341.hook: Cain kills Abel and God still puts a mark of protection on him
341.howItsDone: In the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, the priest asks God to accept the offering as he accepted the gifts of Abel the just, the sacrifice of Abraham and the offering of Melchizedek.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the protoevangelium: a promise tucked inside the serpent's sentence. Your line was the promise came first. Now, outside the garden, the first family.

A line from Genesis gets quoted far from Genesis. A politician uses it in a speech. A teacher writes it on a board. Someone mutters it when asked to help a neighbor: what am I, my brother's keeper? It sounds like a shrug. In Genesis, it's a lie, told to God's face, by a man who has just killed his brother. Two brothers, born outside Eden. One works the soil, one keeps sheep. They both bring an offering. And one of them doesn't come home.
screen: `A LINE PEOPLE QUOTE.` → `IT'S A LIE, TOLD TO GOD.` → `TWO BROTHERS, ONE OFFERING EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the offerings. Cain brings fruit of the ground; Abel brings the firstlings of his flock. God has respect to Abel's offering and not to Cain's. Why? Genesis is silent, and readers have offered guesses; the Letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. Second, the warning. Cain's face falls, and God speaks to him before anything happens: sin lies at the door, but you can master it. Cain doesn't answer. He takes his brother into the field and kills him. Third, the question. As in the garden, God asks what God already knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "Where is thy brother Abel? And he answered, I know not: am I my brother's keeper?" Adam hid. Cain lies, then shrugs. And God says: "The voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." The ground that took Adam's sweat now drinks a brother's blood. The Catechism quotes this scene when it teaches the sacredness of every human life. Fourth, the surprise. Cain is sent out as a wanderer, afraid someone will kill him, and God puts a mark on him: not a brand of shame, but a sign of protection. Nobody is to take his life. Even for a murderer, God keeps the door open. Catholics remember Abel at the altar: the Roman Canon names the offering of Abel the just. Genesis leaves Cain's question hanging. Readers hear the rest of scripture answer it: yes.

342.title: Noah builds (Genesis 6–7)
342.hook: a righteous man builds a boat under a clear sky
342.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the priest's blessing of the baptismal water recalls the flood as a sign of baptism, and Catholics have long pictured the Church as an ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shomer: a lie, a shrug, and a mark of protection. Your line was yes, you are.

A man in a quiet neighborhood starts building a boat in his backyard. Not a canoe: a ship longer than a football field, three decks high, nowhere near any water. Day after day, the sound of saws, for years. The famous retellings of Noah are full of mocking crowds, jokes and a lonely builder. Genesis never mentions a single neighbor's reaction. Not one word. What it gives us instead is a man, an instruction, and a long, plain list of measurements.
screen: `A SHIP IN THE BACKYARD.` → `NO WATER IN SIGHT.` → `GENESIS: NOT ONE NEIGHBOR'S WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the world. By chapter six, the story says the earth is corrupt and filled with violence, and God is grieved at heart. Cain's one murder has become a whole culture. Second, the man. In the Douay-Rheims: "Noe was a just and perfect man in his generations, he walked with God." Noe is the old Latin spelling of Noah, and walked with God is the same phrase Genesis used for Enoch. Third, the instruction. God tells him to make an ark of timber planks, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high, roughly four hundred fifty feet, with rooms, a window and a door in the side. The Hebrew word for ark, tevah, appears in only one other story in the Bible: the little basket the baby Moses floats in on the Nile. A giant ship and a reed basket, the same word, each carrying someone through the water to a new beginning. Fourth, what Noah does, the whole point of the chapter: "And Noe did all things which God commanded him." Genesis says it more than once. No speech, no argument. He builds. Then the rain comes, forty days and forty nights, and the ark lifts off the ground. From early on, Christians read the ark as more than a boat. The First Letter of Peter compares the flood waters to baptism, and Church Fathers saw the ark as the Church, carrying people safely through. The flood is still named in the Easter Vigil's blessing of the baptismal water. A man building under a clear sky, because he trusted the one who told him to.

343.title: The bow in the clouds (Genesis 8–9)
343.hook: after the flood, God's promise with every living thing
343.howItsDone: The Church reads God's covenant with Noah (Genesis 9:8–15) on the First Sunday of Lent in one year of its cycle, and the Catechism describes it as God's covenant with all the nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Noah builds: a ship under a clear sky, and a man who did all things God commanded. Your line was build anyway.

A hundred and fifty days, the water rules the earth. Then it begins to fall. The ark grounds on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven, which flies back and forth. Then a dove, which finds nowhere to land and comes back to his hand. He waits seven days and sends her again, and at evening she returns with an olive leaf in her beak. Seven days more, and she doesn't come back at all. A dove with an olive branch still turns up on flags and posters as a sign of peace. But the story isn't finished when the ground dries.
screen: `A RAVEN, BACK AND FORTH.` → `A DOVE WITH AN OLIVE LEAF.` → `THEN SHE DOESN'T COME BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Covenant, in Hebrew berit, is a binding promise between two parties, more than a contract, closer to a family bond. God promised one to Noah before the flood; here it is made. Second, who's in it: Noah, his sons, their children after them, and, the text keeps saying, every living creature, birds, cattle, beasts of the earth. The animals are partners in a promise. Third, what's promised: never again will a flood destroy the earth. And the sign, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant between me, and between the earth." The Hebrew word for bow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a warrior's bow. Some readers picture God hanging up the weapon, pointed away from the earth; the text doesn't spell that out. But the text is clear about who the sign is for: when the bow appears, God says, I will remember. The reminder is for God. Fourth, why the Church cares. The Catechism places this covenant within God's plan of salvation, and says it stays in force for the nations until the gospel is proclaimed to the whole world. It closes a week that began with a lonely man in a garden: a serpent's question, a call into the trees, the first good news, a brother's blood, an ark, and now color across the sky.

segments.voice: If you can see a window, look out of it now; if not, picture the last sky you noticed, and let your eyes rest on whatever color is there. Then think of every creature under that same sky, birds, a neighbor's dog, a fish you'll never see, a stranger across the world, all inside one promise in the story. If you pray, give thanks for them.
